title: String Methods, Formatting, and Encoding
description: Common string methods for searching, replacing, splitting and joining, plus a first look at Unicode and encoding.
objectives: Use common string methods: search, replace, split, join, case conversion
Understand basic Unicode and text encoding concepts
Choose between split()/join() for text processing tasks

content.heading: Searching, Replacing, Splitting, and Joining
content.body:
Python strings come with a rich set of built-in methods (all of which return new strings, since strings are immutable). For searching: text.find(sub) returns the lowest index of sub, or -1 if absent; text.index(sub) does the same but raises ValueError if not found. For membership without needing a position, use the in operator. text.replace(old, new) returns a copy with every occurrence of old replaced. text.strip() (and lstrip()/rstrip()) remove leading/trailing whitespace (or a specified set of characters).

text.split(sep) breaks a string into a list of substrings around sep (or any whitespace, if sep is omitted); sep.join(iterable) does the reverse, joining a list of strings into one string using sep as glue — this is the idiomatic and efficient way to build a string from many pieces, in contrast to repeated +=. Case conversion methods include upper(), lower(), title(), and capitalize().

content.heading: Unicode and Encoding, Briefly
content.body: Python 3 strings (str) are sequences of Unicode code points — they can represent virtually any character from any writing system, including emoji. When a string needs to be stored in a file or sent over a network, it must be encoded into bytes using a specific encoding, most commonly UTF-8: text.encode("utf-8") produces a bytes object; bytes.decode("utf-8") reverses it back into a str. Mixing up str and bytes (e.g., trying to write a str directly to a file opened in binary mode) is a common source of TypeErrors for beginners working with files or networking.

content.code:
text = "  Hello, World!  "
print(text.strip().lower())        # "hello, world!"

words = "one,two,,three".split(",")
print(words)                        # ['one', 'two', '', 'three']
print("-".join(["a", "b", "c"]))    # "a-b-c"

encoded = "café".encode("utf-8")
print(encoded, encoded.decode("utf-8"))
content.explanation: split(",") keeps an empty string between two consecutive commas — splitting doesn't collapse empty fields unless you filter them out. encode()/decode() round-trip a str through bytes using UTF-8.

keyPoints: String methods always return new strings — they never mutate in place
split()/join() are the idiomatic way to break apart and reassemble text
find()/index() locate substrings; replace() substitutes them
str is Unicode text; bytes is raw binary data — encode()/decode() convert between them
commonMistakes: Using index() when find() (or an in check) would avoid an unwanted ValueError
Building up a large string with += in a loop instead of collecting pieces and using join()
Confusing str and bytes when doing file or network I/O
